newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Bougainville peace talks set to wrap up in NZ.
newsitem.headline: Bougainville peace talks set to wrap up in NZ.

text.p: Talks aimed at ending a nine-year secessionist war on Papua New Guinea's Bougainville Island are likely to end formally on Friday, New Zealand officials said.
"The talks are being wound up today," a foreign ministry official told Reuters.

Leaders from the main factions in the fighting are to hold a news conference later on Friday with New Zealand Foreign Minister Don McKinnon at the Burnham military camp, near the South Island city of Christchurch.
About 70 Bougainville representatives have been in talks at Burnham for the last two weeks, in almost complete isolation.
New Zealand has not been party to the negotiations. The only official statement from the meetings, made a week ago, said broad progress had been made.
Thousands have died in the Bougainville conflict since landowners revolted in 1988 over environmental damage caused by the huge Panguna copper mine, and the royalties they received from it.
The mine is owned by a unit of the Anglo-Australian giant Rio Tinto Ltd.

The rebel Bougainville Revolutionary Army (BRA) leader Joseph Kabui and the PNG-backed Bougainville Transitional Government's (BTG) Premier Gerard Sinato are both expected to address the news conference.
McKinnon has said he did not expect a "quick fix" at the talks, but hoped that the Bougainvilleans could reach a point "where they can in all confidence actively engage with the PNG government".
He has characterised what he hopes will emerge from the talks as "a kind of agreement to a process which will last for quite a while".
The main issues at Burnham have been the same for many years and include the role of the PNG defence force and the assurance of security on the island.
McKinnon said last week he understood there had been some discussions about creating a neutral zone on the island, but gave no further details.
Sources at the talks have said one aim is to seek a zone policed by a Pacific peacekeeping force where substantive peace negotiations can take place.
